## The question

[Area bounded by a curve](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4751824/area-bounded-by-a-curve), asked by [user3.14](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1201323/user3-14) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-08-12; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Question: Find the area bounded by the curve $y$= $4$ $Tan{\frac{x}{2}}$, X-axis (or $y=0$), $x= {\frac{-π}{2}}$ and $x= {\frac{-π}{3}}$.
>
> I am having a slight difference in the answer and I am not able to figure out why it's happening. I hope I get it resolved through this post.
>
> My solution:
>
> Sketch the graph first. For $y$= $4$ $Tan{\frac{x}{2}}$, lets check the periodicity. 
> Periodicity= $2π$, then for different values of x, the graph of $y$= $4$ $Tan{\frac{x}{2}}$ out to be:
>
> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
>
> Since periodicity =$2π$, so lets only take the portion of the graph from $x=-π$ to $x=π$.
>
> [![enter image description here][q-2]][q-2]
>
> We need to find the shaded area from $x=-\frac{π}{2}$ to $x=-\frac{π}{3}$. The following is the required area:
>
>
> [![enter image description here][q-3]][q-3]
>
>
>   [q-1]: MdOMR.png
>   [q-2]: VV2It.png
>   [q-3]: WcONx.png
>
> Shaded Area is: 
>
> $\int _{−π/2 }^{−π/3 }$ $4$ $Tan{\frac{x}{2}}$dx
>
> = $8$ $ln|sec \frac{x}{2}|$ from $x=-\frac{π}{2}$ to $x=-\frac{π}{3}$
>
> = $8$ ($ln|sec \frac{-\frac{π}{3}}{2}|$ - $ln|sec \frac{-\frac{π}{2}}{2}|$)
>
> = $8$ $ln|\frac {sec \frac{-\frac{π}{3}}{2}} {sec \frac{-\frac{π}{2}}{2}}|$
>
> = $8$ $ln|\frac {sec \frac{-π}{6}} {sec \frac{-π}{4}}|$
>
> = $8$ $ln|\frac {sec \frac{π}{6}} {sec \frac{π}{4}}|$
>
> = $8$ $\ln \left| \frac{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}}{\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}} \right|$ 
>
> = $8$ $\ln \left| \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \right|$ 
>
> Now, the answer mentioned in the exercise is $8$ $\ln \left| \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}\right|$ and this is true when:
>
> $\int _{−π/2 }^{−π/3 }$ $4$ $Tan{\frac{x}{2}}$dx = $-8$ $ln|cos \frac{x}{2}|$ from $x=-\frac{π}{2}$ to $x=-\frac{π}{3}$
>
> Why does this difference in answer occur? I think that it might be because the shaded area is below the X-axis and thus should come out to be negative and ultimately the value is taken ignoring the negative sign. Thus, $\int _{−π/2 }^{−π/3 }$ $4$ $Tan{\frac{x}{2}}$dx should be equal to $-8$ $ln|cos \frac{x}{2}|$ from $x=-\frac{π}{2}$ to $x=-\frac{π}{3}$ instead of $8$ $ln|sec \frac{x}{2}|$ from $x=-\frac{π}{2}$ to $x=-\frac{π}{3}$.
>
> Is my interpretation and calculation correct? Please help with the problem regarding the difference in the answer. Is my reasoning correct for it? Looking forward to your response.
>
> Thank you.
:::

In addition to the sign of the definite integral, it seems you are worried about the difference between the functions $-8 \ln |\cos(x/2)|$ and $8 \ln|\sec(x/2)|$.

Those are, in fact, equivalent since $- \ln z = \ln (z^{-1}) = \ln \frac{1}{z}$ for any $z$. Also, $\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}$. So 
$$8 \ln|\sec(x/2)| = 8 \ln\left|\frac{1}{\cos(x/2)}\right|
   =-8 \ln|\cos(x/2)|$$
